Q: Creating a sequence in python 3 A:

First of all, your indentation inside the loop should throw an error.

Recursion

For the Fibonacci sequence where xᵢ = xᵢ₋₁ = xᵢ₋₂ with x₀ = x₁ = 1, you can use the following recursive function:

def fib(num: int) -> int:
  if num <= 1:
    return 1  # first two numbers
  return fib(num - 1) + fib(num - 2)

To start with another number at the first two indices, set the value of the first return statement in the function to your desired starting point.

Recursions can cause a stack overflow and are rather primitive, but for this purpose it doesn't matter too much.

The real Fibonacci sequence starts with x₀ = 0 and x₁ = 1. This brings us closer to the more flexibel function, that can also calculate a number from the Lucas sequence, which follows the same rule but starts with x₀ = 2 and x₁ = 1.

def luc(num: int) -> int:
  if num <= 0:
    return 2  # first starting number
  if num == 1:
    return 1  # second starting number
  return luc(num - 1) luc(num - 2)

To set starting numbers, change the numbers from the first two return statements.

To make the function even less hard-coded, you can also take your starting values as arguments. Let's rename the default number num to idx for index, since it's the number at the given index in the sequence. Now the function has three parameters:

def seq(idx: int, x0: int, x1: int) -> int:
  if idx <= 0:
    return x0
  if idx == 1:
    return x1
  return seq(idx - 1, x0, x1) seq(idx - 2, x0, x1)

The arguments get passed on unnecessarily, since the starting values don't change inside the function. The cleaner looking version would be:

def sequence(idx: int, x0: int, x1: int) -> int:
  def seq(idx) -> int:
    if idx <= 0:
      return x0
    if idx == 1:
      return x1
    return seq (idx)

  return seq(idx)

But the recursive approach has a time complexity of O(2n) and a space complexity of O(n). In short: it scales pretty badly and gets very expensive really quickly.

Loop

The approach with a loop follows the same rule, but it looks completely different. There is no need for a function, but it's cleaner, reusable and the code won't be as hard-coded as with the raw loop.

def sequence(idx: int, x0: int, x1: int) -> int:
  if idx <= 0:
    return x0
  if idx == 1:
    return x1

  a = x0
  b = x1

  for _ int range(1, idx):
    sum = a + b
    a = b
    b = sum

  return sum

Or even more concise:

def sequence(idx: int, x0: int, x1: int) -> int:
  if idx <= 0:
    return x0
  if idx == 1:
    return x1

  a = x0
  b = x1

  for _ int range(1, idx):
    a, b = b, a + b

  return b

The loop approach has the advantage, that it has a time complexity of O(n) and a space complexity of O(1).

This can be even easier to read if you know how:

_ in a loop is still the same as any other name for an item in a sequence, but it suggests, that the items aren't used inside the loop.

The syntax inside the loop a, b = b, a + b is called multiple assignment and just a combination of tuple packing and sequence unpacking (for further reading, visit the docs).

Q: PostgreSQL rename table - cascade renaming to objects like indices, constraints that contain table name A:

This will rename any index which name not following $tableName_$columnName(composite index will concat each name of column component with _), primary key index for $tableName_pkey and other rules for constraint name: PostgreSQL: default constraint names, note it's possible to override the default rule when CREATE TABLE: PostgreSQL: is it possible to provide custom name for PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE?

-- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65069778/postgresql-rename-table-cascade-renaming-to-objects-like-indices-constraints/78485773#78485773
DO
$do$
DECLARE
    r record;
    target_schema text := 'your_schema';
BEGIN
    FOR r IN
        SELECT format('ALTER INDEX %I RENAME TO %I', "index", new_index) sql, *
        FROM (
            SELECT "table", "index",
                   format('%s%s_%s',
                          "table",
                          CASE constraint_type
                              -- only uncomment below line when using postgresql<12 https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4107915/postgresql-default-constraint-names#comment109084417_4108266
                              -- WHEN 'f' THEN '_' || "column"[1] -- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4107915/postgresql-default-constraint-names#comment127573826_4108266
                              WHEN 'p' THEN '' -- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4107915/postgresql-default-constraint-names#comment127553786_4108266
                              ELSE '_' || string_agg("column", '_')
                          END,
                          CASE coalesce(constraint_type, 'NULL') -- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/15417167/case-when-null-evaluates-to-false
                              -- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4107915/postgresql-default-constraint-names/4108266#4108266
                              -- https://gist.github.com/popravich/d6816ef1653329fb1745
                              -- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/8674562/postgresql-is-it-possible-to-provide-custom-name-for-primary-key-or-unique/8674640#8674640
                              WHEN 'c' THEN 'check'
                              WHEN 'f' THEN 'fkey'
                              WHEN 'p' THEN 'pkey'
                              WHEN 'u' THEN 'key'
                              WHEN 'x' THEN 'excl'
                              WHEN 'NULL' THEN 'idx'
                          END
                   ) new_index
            FROM (
                SELECT ct.relname "table", ci.relname "index", c.contype constraint_type, a.attname "column"
                FROM pg_index i -- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/37329561/how-to-list-indexes-created-for-table-in-postgres/37330092#37330092
                JOIN pg_class ct ON ct.oid = i.indrelid
                JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = ct.relnamespace
                JOIN pg_class ci ON ci.oid = i.indexrelid
                JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = ANY(i.indkey) AND a.attnum > 0 -- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/55447819/how-to-get-the-list-of-column-names-for-all-indexes-on-a-table-in-postgresql/55448707#55448707
                LEFT JOIN pg_constraint c ON c.conindid = i.indexrelid -- https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/catalog-pg-constraint.html
                WHERE n.nspname = target_schema
            ) t
            GROUP BY "table", "index", constraint_type
        ) t
        WHERE "index" != new_index
    LOOP
        -- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1348126/postgresql-modify-owner-on-all-tables-simultaneously-in-postgresql/37259655#37259655
        RAISE NOTICE '%', r.sql; -- dry-run
        -- EXECUTE r.sql; -- uncomment to run them
        COMMIT; -- https://dba.stackexchange.com/questions/315063/disable-toast-compression-for-all-columns/315067#315067
    END LOOP;
END
$do$

Q: How to mark an Airflow DAG run as failed if any task fails? A:

for airflow v3 ->

from airflow.providers.standard.operators.empty import EmptyOperator
from airflow.providers.standard.operators.python import PythonOperator
from airflow.sdk import TaskInstanceState, TriggerRule, get_current_context
from airflow.sdk import DAG, CronDataIntervalTimetable, timezone

with DAG(
    dag_id="test_dag_run",
    schedule=CronDataIntervalTimetable("0 0 1 * *", "Europe/Paris"),
    start_date=timezone.parse("2026-07-05T00:00:00", "Europe/Paris"),
    catchup=False,
):
    task_1 = EmptyOperator(
        task_id="Empty",
    )


    def final_status_callable():
        context = get_current_context()
        ti = context["ti"]
        dag_run = context["dag_run"]

        states_by_run = ti.get_task_states(
            dag_id=ti.dag_id,
            run_ids=[dag_run.run_id],
        )
        task_states = states_by_run.get(dag_run.run_id, {})

        print(f"Status of all tasks for dag_run {dag_run.run_id!r}:")
        failed_tasks = []

        for task_id, state in sorted(task_states.items()):
            if task_id == ti.task_id:
                continue  # this task itself is still "running"
            print(f"  {task_id:<30} {state}")

            if state in (TaskInstanceState.FAILED, TaskInstanceState.UPSTREAM_FAILED):
                failed_tasks.append(task_id)

        if failed_tasks:
            raise RuntimeError(f"These tasks did not succeed: {failed_tasks}")


    task_2 = final_status = PythonOperator(
        task_id="final_status",
        python_callable=final_status_callable,
        trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ALL_DONE,
    )

    task_1 >> task_2

Q: How to expose a multi-model, case-scoped "detail" read in DRF without adding a new endpoint? A:

I think your reasoning is pretty sound. I wouldn't use ?tab_name=creditSummary here either. Since creditSummary is really identifying which sub-resource you're asking for, I'd put it in the path.

Something like this seems perfectly reasonable:

path("cases/<uuid:case_uuid>/records/", RecordsView.as_view()),

path("cases/<uuid:case_uuid>/records/<str:tab_name>/", RecordsView.as_view()),

and then have GET call something like TabReadService.read(tab_name, case).

I don't think having the same view handle both is inherently a problem either. The fact that the existing class was originally written for POST doesn't mean it can't grow a GET if both operations belong to the same URL/resource.

The part I'd be a little more careful about is the service layer. Since the GET is doing a fairly specific aggregation of the latest A + latest B and reshaping the response, I'd keep that logic out of the view entirely. The view should basically just resolve the case/tab and hand it off to the read service.

I also wouldn't introduce a ViewSet/custom action just for the sake of being "more DRF". A ViewSet makes more sense if you're actually modelling a resource with the usual CRUD operations or several related actions. In your case, the existing URL structure already has a concept of records, and the tab is effectively a named sub-resource.

One thing I'd probably add is validation for tab_name rather than letting an arbitrary string reach the service:

service = TAB_READ_SERVICES.get(tab_name)

if not service:

raise NotFound("Unknown tab")

That also keeps the closed-enum behaviour explicit.

So I'd probably go with the second URL you proposed. It's consistent with the rest of the API, doesn't change the existing POST contract, and makes the GET endpoint pretty obvious from the URL. The fact that the response is built from multiple models doesn't really require a separate endpoint by itself.
